course.title: Quantitative Reasoning and Data Literacy
course.description: Develops practical statistical reasoning, data interpretation and evidence-aware decision making for students across disciplines.

outcomes.text: Classify data types, assess data quality and prepare small datasets for analysis.
Summarize distributions using appropriate descriptive statistics and visualizations.
Interpret probability, sampling, uncertainty and statistical claims without overstating conclusions.
Detect misleading graphs, percentages, averages and unsupported causal claims.
Produce a concise evidence brief from a real dataset with transparent calculations and limitations.

lessons.title: Variables, observations and measurement scales
lessons.teaching_material: A dataset represents observations about units such as people, firms, countries or events. Variables describe attributes of those units. Categorical variables encode groups or labels, while quantitative variables represent numeric measurements for which arithmetic may be meaningful. Measurement scale matters because it determines which summaries and comparisons are defensible. A numeric code assigned to categories is still categorical if the numbers do not represent measurable magnitude.
lessons.activity: Inspect a small public dataset and classify ten fields by unit of analysis, variable type and plausible measurement scale.

self_check.q: Is a postcode a quantitative variable because it contains numbers?
self_check.a: No. It is usually a categorical identifier because arithmetic on the code is not meaningful.

self_check.q: What is the unit of analysis?
self_check.a: The entity about which each observation is recorded and conclusions are drawn.

lessons.title: Missingness, validity and data provenance
lessons.teaching_material: Data quality includes validity, completeness, consistency, timeliness and fitness for purpose. Missing values may arise systematically rather than randomly, so simply deleting them can distort results. Provenance records where data came from, how it was collected, what definitions were used and what transformations were applied. A transparent analysis keeps original data separate from cleaned data and records every consequential change so another analyst can reconstruct the process.
lessons.activity: Create a data-quality log for a sample dataset listing missing values, impossible values, duplicates, inconsistent labels and proposed treatment.

self_check.q: Why can deleting all incomplete rows be risky?
self_check.a: If missingness is systematic, deletion can change the composition of the sample and bias results.

self_check.q: What does provenance protect?
self_check.a: Traceability of source, definitions, collection and transformations.

lessons.title: Center, spread and shape
objectives: Choose summaries suited to distribution shape
lessons.teaching_material: The mean uses every value and is sensitive to extremes; the median identifies the middle ordered value and is more robust to outliers. Spread can be described with range, interquartile range, variance or standard deviation. No single statistic describes a distribution completely. Analysts should examine center, spread, shape and unusual values together and choose summaries that fit both the data type and the distribution's characteristics.
lessons.activity: Compare mean, median, range and interquartile range for two income distributions before and after adding one extreme value.

self_check.q: Which measure of center is usually more resistant to extreme outliers?
self_check.a: The median.

self_check.q: Why report spread as well as center?
self_check.a: Two datasets can have the same center while differing greatly in variability and practical meaning.

lessons.title: Percentages, rates and denominators
objectives: Distinguish percentage points from percent change
lessons.teaching_material: Percentages are ratios and are meaningful only when the denominator is clear. A rise from 20% to 25% is an increase of 5 percentage points but a 25% relative increase. Rates may incorporate exposure such as population, time or transactions, allowing fairer comparison between groups of different sizes. Large relative changes can also be misleading when the starting value is very small, so absolute quantities should often be reported alongside relative measures.
lessons.activity: Rewrite five statistical headlines so each states the denominator, absolute change and relative change where relevant.

self_check.q: What is the difference between percentage points and percent change?
self_check.a: Percentage points subtract percentages directly; percent change divides the change by the starting percentage.

self_check.q: Why can relative risk alone mislead?
self_check.a: A large relative change may correspond to a very small absolute change when the baseline risk is low.

lessons.title: Probability and conditional reasoning
lessons.teaching_material: Probability quantifies uncertainty under a stated model or long-run process. Conditional probability asks how likely an event is given additional information, and it can differ greatly from the reverse condition. Base rates matter: even an accurate test can generate many false positives when the underlying condition is rare. Good quantitative reasoning therefore states the reference class, condition and denominator rather than treating percentages as context-free facts.
lessons.activity: Work through a screening-test example using a 10,000-person frequency table to calculate true positives, false positives and the probability of the condition after a positive result.

self_check.q: Is P(A given B) generally equal to P(B given A)?
self_check.a: No. Reversing the condition changes the probability and often produces a very different value.

self_check.q: Why do base rates matter?
self_check.a: They determine how common the underlying condition is and strongly affect the interpretation of test results.

lessons.title: Samples, bias and margins of error
objectives: Evaluate whether a sample supports population inference
lessons.teaching_material: A sample can differ from a population through random sampling variation and through systematic bias. Increasing sample size reduces random error but does not repair a biased sampling frame, leading question or nonresponse pattern. A margin of error describes sampling uncertainty under assumptions; it does not include every source of error. Population inference is strongest when the sample was selected using a defensible process and when nonresponse and coverage are examined.
lessons.activity: Audit three survey scenarios for sampling frame, selection method, nonresponse risk and whether a reported margin of error is meaningful.

self_check.q: Does a very large convenience sample guarantee representativeness?
self_check.a: No. Large size reduces random error but cannot eliminate systematic selection bias.

self_check.q: What does a margin of error usually omit?
self_check.a: Nonsampling errors such as measurement bias, coverage problems and nonresponse bias.

lessons.title: Choosing and auditing charts
objectives: Match chart type to analytical question
lessons.teaching_material: Charts should make a comparison, distribution, relationship or change easier to understand. Bar charts commonly compare categories, line charts emphasize change over ordered time, scatterplots show relationships between quantitative variables, and histograms show distributions. Truncated axes, unequal intervals, inappropriate three-dimensional effects and area encodings can exaggerate differences. Labels, units and source notes are part of the evidence, not decoration.
lessons.activity: Redesign two misleading charts and write a short explanation of how the original encoding changed the perceived conclusion.

self_check.q: When is a scatterplot appropriate?
self_check.a: When examining the relationship between two quantitative variables across observations.

self_check.q: Why can a truncated bar-chart axis mislead?
self_check.a: It can visually exaggerate small differences in bar length.

lessons.title: Correlation, confounding and causal language
objectives: Identify plausible confounders and reverse causality
lessons.teaching_material: Correlation describes association, not the mechanism that produced it. Two variables may move together because one affects the other, because causality runs in the opposite direction, because a third variable influences both, or by coincidence. Causal claims require design and evidence that address these alternatives. Observational data can still be valuable, but conclusions should use language proportional to what the design supports and should identify plausible confounders.
lessons.activity: For four observed correlations, propose at least two alternative explanations and rewrite causal headlines into evidence-appropriate language.

self_check.q: What is confounding?
self_check.a: A third factor is related to both the exposure and outcome and can create or distort the observed association.

self_check.q: Can observational evidence ever contribute to causal reasoning?
self_check.a: Yes, but stronger assumptions, methods and converging evidence are needed than a simple correlation alone.

lessons.title: Spreadsheet analysis and reproducible calculations
objectives: Separate raw data from analysis outputs
lessons.teaching_material: A reproducible spreadsheet keeps raw data intact, uses explicit formulas rather than manually typed derived values, labels units and assumptions, and avoids hidden transformations. Structured tables, data validation and named calculations reduce error. Important results should be cross-checked using an independent calculation where feasible. Reproducibility means another person can follow the workbook and understand how the reported value was obtained from the source data.
lessons.activity: Build a small analysis workbook with raw-data, cleaning-log, calculations and findings sheets, then ask a peer to reproduce one reported statistic.

self_check.q: Why avoid overwriting raw data?
self_check.a: It preserves the original evidence and allows cleaning decisions to be audited or reversed.

self_check.q: What makes a spreadsheet calculation transparent?
self_check.a: Visible formulas, clear labels, documented assumptions and traceable source cells.

lessons.title: Writing an evidence-aware data brief
objectives: Translate analysis into a concise finding
lessons.teaching_material: A data brief should answer a defined question, explain the dataset and method briefly, present only the analyses needed for that question, and distinguish observed results from interpretation. Visuals should be directly tied to claims. Limitations such as missing data, sample coverage, measurement definition or inability to infer causality must be visible. A strong conclusion states what decision the evidence informs without pretending the data answer questions they were not designed to answer.
lessons.activity: Produce a two-page data brief from an open dataset with one table, two charts, three findings, one limitation section and a reproducible calculation appendix.

self_check.q: Why separate result from interpretation?
self_check.a: The observed statistic and the explanation for why it occurred are different claims requiring different support.

self_check.q: What should a limitation section do?
self_check.a: Explain material constraints that affect confidence, generalizability or interpretation of the findings.

assessments.title: Statistical Claim Audit
assessments.instructions: Audit five public quantitative claims for denominator, measurement, uncertainty, visualization and causal language.

assessments.title: Data Analysis Workbook
assessments.instructions: Submit a reproducible spreadsheet using a real open dataset, including raw data, cleaning log, formulas, descriptive analysis and visualizations.

assessments.title: Evidence-Aware Data Brief
assessments.instructions: Produce a two-page decision-oriented brief from the workbook with transparent findings, uncertainty and limitations.
